title: Money & Consumption
subtitle: Build a budget, buy with a conscience and spot the scam before it costs you

lessons.title: Le budget
lessons.description: Talk about where your money actually goes: fixed charges, variable spending, savings goals and the vocabulary French people use when the month is longer than the salary.

blocks.heading: Fixed charges versus variable spending
blocks.body: A French budget splits in two. Les charges fixes are the amounts that leave your account whether you like it or not — rent, insurance, subscriptions, the phone plan. Les dépenses variables are everything you decide month by month: food, going out, clothes. The verb for the whole exercise is gérer son budget, and the two amounts that matter are ce qui rentre (what comes in) and ce qui sort (what goes out).

examples.french: Mes charges fixes représentent presque soixante pour cent de mon salaire.
examples.english: My fixed costs come to almost sixty percent of my salary.

examples.french: Le loyer et l'assurance partent par prélèvement automatique le 5.
examples.english: The rent and the insurance go out by direct debit on the 5th.

examples.french: Je gère mon budget dans un simple tableur.
examples.english: I manage my budget in a simple spreadsheet.

examples.french: Les dépenses variables, c'est là que ça dérape.
examples.english: Variable spending — that's where it goes off the rails.

examples.french: Chaque mois, je note ce qui rentre et ce qui sort.
examples.english: Every month I write down what comes in and what goes out.

examples.french: J'ai résilié deux abonnements que je n'utilisais plus.
examples.english: I cancelled two subscriptions I wasn't using any more.

blocks.tip: Charges on its own almost always means recurring costs, not "charges" in the sense of fees. A bank fee is des frais bancaires.

blocks.heading: Saying you are short — without saying pauvre
blocks.body: French has a whole register of half-joking expressions for running out of money before the end of the month. Être fauché is the everyday one, joindre les deux bouts is the neutral idiom for making ends meet, and se serrer la ceinture means cutting back. Être à découvert is the concrete banking version: your account has gone below zero.

examples.french: Je suis fauché jusqu'au 30, désolé.
examples.english: I'm broke until the 30th, sorry.

examples.french: Avec un seul salaire, on a du mal à joindre les deux bouts.
examples.english: On one salary, we struggle to make ends meet.

examples.french: Il va falloir se serrer la ceinture cette année.
examples.english: We're going to have to tighten our belts this year.

examples.french: Je me retrouve à découvert tous les 25 du mois.
examples.english: I end up overdrawn on the 25th of every month.

examples.french: Ce mois-ci, j'ai un imprévu : le dentiste.
examples.english: This month I've had an unexpected expense: the dentist.

examples.french: Elle est économe, mais elle n'est pas radine.
examples.english: She's thrifty, but she isn't stingy.

blocks.tip: Économe is a compliment; radin or pingre is an insult. The difference matters at a dinner table.

blocks.heading: Setting a savings goal
blocks.body: To talk about saving, French distinguishes économiser (to save money by spending less) from épargner (to set money aside, often on a savings account). Mettre de côté is the everyday phrase for both. A target is un objectif, and the amount you put aside each month is what you mets de côté. Use pour + infinitive or pour que + subjunctive to give the purpose.

examples.french: Je mets deux cents euros de côté chaque mois.
examples.english: I put two hundred euros aside every month.

examples.french: Mon objectif, c'est d'avoir trois mois de salaire d'épargne.
examples.english: My goal is to have three months' salary in savings.

examples.french: J'économise sur les courses pour pouvoir partir en août.
examples.english: I'm saving on the shopping so I can go away in August.

examples.french: On épargne pour l'apport d'un appartement.
examples.english: We're saving for the deposit on a flat.

examples.french: Le virement vers mon livret est automatique, je n'y pense plus.
examples.english: The transfer to my savings account is automatic, I don't think about it any more.

examples.french: À ce rythme-là, j'aurai la somme dans deux ans.
examples.english: At this rate, I'll have the sum in two years.

blocks.tip: Un livret A is the standard tax-free French savings account — almost everyone has one, so the word comes up constantly.

blocks.heading: Si + imparfait → conditionnel : budgeting hypotheses
blocks.body: To imagine a different financial situation, French uses si + imperfect in one half and the present conditional in the other. Never put a conditional after si. The order can be reversed without changing the meaning, and this pattern is the natural way to weigh up a decision out loud.

examples.french: Si je résiliais deux abonnements, j'économiserais trente euros par mois.
examples.english: If I cancelled two subscriptions, I'd save thirty euros a month.

examples.french: Je mettrais plus de côté si mon loyer était moins élevé.
examples.english: I'd put more aside if my rent were lower.

examples.french: Si on cuisinait plus souvent, on dépenserait moins en livraisons.
examples.english: If we cooked more often, we'd spend less on deliveries.

examples.french: Qu'est-ce que tu ferais si tu recevais une prime ?
examples.english: What would you do if you got a bonus?

examples.french: Si tu étais à découvert, tu paierais des frais bancaires.
examples.english: If you were overdrawn, you'd pay bank charges.

examples.french: Ce serait plus simple si le virement était automatique.
examples.english: It would be simpler if the transfer were automatic.

blocks.tip: Careful with spelling: si + il becomes s'il, but si + elle stays si elle.

blocks.heading: The pronoun en with amounts
blocks.body: En replaces de + noun, and it is everywhere in money talk because amounts are always partitive. When you keep the quantity, the number or expression of quantity stays at the end: j'en mets deux cents de côté. En goes before the verb, and in the passé composé the past participle does not agree with it.

examples.french: — Tu as de l'épargne ? — Oui, j'en ai un peu.
examples.english: "Do you have savings?" "Yes, I have a bit."

examples.french: Des dettes ? Je n'en ai plus depuis mars.
examples.english: Debts? I haven't had any since March.

examples.french: Il gagne bien sa vie, mais il en dépense la moitié en loyer.
examples.english: He earns a good living, but he spends half of it on rent.

examples.french: Sur mille euros, j'en mets deux cents de côté.
examples.english: Out of a thousand euros, I put two hundred aside.

examples.french: Des imprévus, on en a tous les mois.
examples.english: Unexpected costs — we get them every month.

examples.french: J'en ai parlé à ma conseillère bancaire.
examples.english: I talked about it with my bank adviser.

blocks.tip: Watch the difference: j'y pense (I'm thinking about it, penser à) but j'en parle (I'm talking about it, parler de).

passages.title: Le tableur de Malika
passages.french:
Depuis janvier, Malika tient un tableur où elle note tout, jusqu'au café du matin.
Au début, elle trouvait ça pénible ; aujourd'hui, ça lui prend cinq minutes le dimanche soir.
La première surprise a été le poste « livraisons » : cent quarante euros en un mois.
« Je croyais que mon problème, c'était le loyer », dit-elle. « En fait, c'était les petites dépenses. »
Elle a donc résilié deux abonnements qu'elle n'utilisait plus et réduit les commandes à une par semaine.
Ses charges fixes, elles, n'ont pas bougé : loyer, assurance, transport, téléphone.
« Sur ces lignes-là, je ne peux rien faire avant de déménager », explique-t-elle.
Le 2 de chaque mois, un virement automatique envoie deux cents euros vers son livret.
« Si j'attendais la fin du mois pour épargner, il ne resterait jamais rien. »
Son objectif : trois mois de salaire de côté, pour ne plus paniquer devant un imprévu.
Elle en est à la moitié, et elle avoue qu'elle regarde son relevé bancaire avec beaucoup moins d'angoisse.
« Je ne suis pas devenue radine », précise-t-elle en riant. « Je suis juste devenue économe. »
passages.english:
Since January, Malika has kept a spreadsheet where she notes everything, down to the morning coffee.
At first she found it a chore; today it takes her five minutes on Sunday evening.
The first surprise was the "deliveries" category: a hundred and forty euros in one month.
"I thought my problem was the rent," she says. "Actually, it was the small expenses."
So she cancelled two subscriptions she wasn't using any more and cut orders down to one a week.
Her fixed costs, on the other hand, haven't budged: rent, insurance, transport, phone.
"On those lines I can't do anything until I move," she explains.
On the 2nd of every month, an automatic transfer sends two hundred euros to her savings account.
"If I waited until the end of the month to save, there would never be anything left."
Her goal: three months' salary set aside, so as not to panic in front of an unexpected expense.
She's halfway there, and she admits she looks at her bank statement with a lot less anxiety.
"I haven't become stingy," she points out, laughing. "I've just become thrifty."

lessons.title: La consommation responsable
lessons.description: Buy second-hand, shop short supply chains, cut waste — and defend your choices in French without sounding like a pamphlet.

blocks.heading: Seconde main : the vocabulary of buying used
blocks.body: France buys second-hand enthusiastically, and each channel has its own word. Une friperie is a second-hand clothes shop, un vide-grenier is a neighbourhood car-boot sale, une brocante is a flea market with dealers. Online, everyone says Le Bon Coin or Vinted. The adjective is d'occasion, and the noun phrase la seconde main is now standard in adverts.

examples.french: J'achète presque tous mes vêtements en seconde main.
examples.english: I buy nearly all my clothes second-hand.

examples.french: J'ai trouvé cette table d'occasion pour vingt euros.
examples.english: I found this second-hand table for twenty euros.

examples.french: Dimanche, il y a un vide-grenier place de la mairie.
examples.english: On Sunday there's a car-boot sale in the town hall square.

examples.french: On chine dans les brocantes le week-end.
examples.english: We hunt for bargains at flea markets at the weekend.

examples.french: L'appareil est reconditionné, avec un an de garantie.
examples.english: The device is refurbished, with a one-year warranty.

examples.french: Plutôt que de jeter, je revends ou je donne.
examples.english: Rather than throwing things out, I resell or give away.

blocks.tip: Chiner is the verb for browsing markets in search of a find; un chineur is someone who does it. It has no real English equivalent.

blocks.heading: Circuits courts and where food comes from
blocks.body: Un circuit court means as few intermediaries as possible between the producer and you: the market, a farm shop, or an AMAP, a subscription box scheme run with local farmers. The arguments you will hear are about supporting le producteur, eating de saison, and cutting l'empreinte carbone. Labels matter too: bio for organic, équitable for fair trade.

examples.french: Je fais mes courses en circuit court depuis deux ans.
examples.english: I've been shopping short supply chains for two years.

examples.french: Ce fromage vient directement du producteur.
examples.english: This cheese comes straight from the producer.

examples.french: On est inscrits à une AMAP : un panier par semaine.

examples.french: J'essaie de manger des fruits de saison.

examples.french: Un kiwi de Nouvelle-Zélande en janvier, ça a une empreinte carbone énorme.
examples.english: A kiwi from New Zealand in January has an enormous carbon footprint.

blocks.tip: In a market, demander l'origine is normal and expected: « Ils viennent d'où, vos poireaux ? » Nobody will find it rude.

blocks.heading: Waste, packaging and buying less
blocks.body: The greener half of the topic is about not buying at all. Le gaspillage is waste as a habit, un déchet is a piece of rubbish, and acheter en vrac means buying loose, without packaging. The rhetorical move French speakers make is to distinguish un besoin from une envie — a need from a want — before deciding.

examples.french: Le gaspillage alimentaire me rend dingue.
examples.english: Food waste drives me crazy.

examples.french: J'achète le riz et les pâtes en vrac.

examples.french: On produit beaucoup moins de déchets depuis qu'on composte.
examples.english: We produce far less rubbish since we started composting.

examples.english: I get my shoes repaired instead of buying new ones.

blocks.tip: Faire réparer quelque chose (to have something repaired) is far more common than réparer quelque chose when you are not doing it yourself.

blocks.heading: The relative pronoun dont
blocks.body: Dont replaces de + noun inside a relative clause. Use it whenever the verb or expression in that clause takes de: avoir besoin de, parler de, être fier de, s'occuper de. It also expresses possession, where English uses whose. Word order after dont is always subject + verb — never invert.

blocks.heading: Comparing quantities and describing a trend
blocks.body: Comparisons of quantity use plus de / moins de / autant de + noun + que. For a trend that keeps going, French uses de plus en plus (de) and de moins en moins (de). Notice that with nouns you always need de after the comparative word, but with adjectives you don't: moins cher, moins de déchets.

passages.title: Six mois sans rien acheter de neuf
passages.french:
En janvier, Yann et Camille se sont lancé un défi : six mois sans acheter un seul objet neuf.
Seules exceptions autorisées : la nourriture, les médicaments et les sous-vêtements.
« Au début, on a cru que ce serait un enfer », raconte Camille. « En réalité, le plus dur, c'est la première semaine. »
Pour la vaisselle et les meubles, ils ont écumé les brocantes et les vide-greniers du département.
Le grille-pain est mort en mars : ils en ont trouvé un reconditionné à quinze euros.
Les vêtements viennent de deux friperies et d'un site de seconde main dont Camille dit le plus grand bien.
« On achète de moins en moins par réflexe », explique Yann. « On attend, et souvent l'envie passe. »
Ils ont aussi organisé un troc entre voisins : chacun apporte ce dont il ne se sert plus.
Le bilan financier les a surpris : presque deux mille euros économisés en six mois.
Le bilan écologique aussi, même s'il est plus difficile à chiffrer : beaucoup moins d'emballages, presque plus de livraisons.
« Je ne fais la morale à personne », insiste Camille. « On ne sauve pas la planète à deux. »
Le défi est terminé depuis juillet, mais ils n'ont, pour l'instant, repris aucune de leurs anciennes habitudes.
passages.english:
In January, Yann and Camille set themselves a challenge: six months without buying a single new object.
The only exceptions allowed: food, medicine and underwear.
"At first we thought it would be hell," says Camille. "In reality, the hardest part is the first week."
For crockery and furniture, they combed the flea markets and car-boot sales of the whole department.
The toaster died in March: they found a refurbished one for fifteen euros.
The clothes come from two second-hand shops and a resale site that Camille speaks very highly of.
"We buy less and less out of reflex," Yann explains. "We wait, and often the urge passes."
They also organised a swap among neighbours: everyone brings what they no longer use.
The financial result surprised them: nearly two thousand euros saved in six months.
The environmental result too, even if it's harder to quantify: far less packaging, almost no more deliveries.
"I'm not lecturing anyone," Camille insists. "Two people don't save the planet."
The challenge ended in July, but so far they haven't gone back to any of their old habits.

lessons.title: Les arnaques
lessons.description: Recognise the classic French scams, warn a friend with il vaut mieux que + subjunctive, and know what to say at the bank and the police station once you've been had.

blocks.heading: Naming the scam
blocks.body: Une arnaque is the everyday word for a rip-off or a scam; une escroquerie is its formal, legal equivalent, and un escroc is the person behind it. Online, l'hameçonnage (phishing) is the official term, though most people say le phishing. The key verb pair is arnaquer quelqu'un (to scam someone) and se faire avoir (to get had), which is what victims actually say.

examples.french: C'est une arnaque classique, ne réponds pas.
examples.english: It's a classic scam, don't reply.

examples.french: Je me suis fait avoir comme un débutant.
examples.english: I got had like a complete beginner.

examples.french: Il s'est fait arnaquer de trois cents euros sur un site de petites annonces.
examples.english: He got scammed out of three hundred euros on a classifieds site.

examples.french: L'escroc se faisait passer pour un conseiller bancaire.
examples.english: The conman was pretending to be a bank adviser.

examples.french: Ce SMS est une tentative d'hameçonnage.
examples.english: This text message is a phishing attempt.

examples.french: Ils vendent des contrefaçons au prix du neuf.
examples.english: They sell counterfeits at full price.

blocks.tip: Se faire + infinitive is the standard way to say something was done to you: se faire voler, se faire arnaquer, se faire rembourser.

blocks.heading: Warning someone: se méfier de and friends
blocks.body: Se méfier de means to be wary of, and it takes de before the thing or person. Méfie-toi ! on its own is a complete warning. Related tools are faire attention à (to watch out for), avoir des doutes sur (to have doubts about) and the noun la méfiance. To describe the person, the adjective is méfiant.

examples.french: Méfie-toi des offres trop belles pour être vraies.
examples.english: Be wary of offers that are too good to be true.

examples.french: Je me méfie de tous les messages qui demandent un code.

examples.english: A little wariness never does any harm.

examples.french: Elle est méfiante depuis qu'elle s'est fait avoir.
examples.english: She has been distrustful since she got scammed.

blocks.tip: Don't confuse se méfier de (to be wary of) with se fier à (to trust). One letter, opposite meaning.

blocks.heading: What to do once it has happened
blocks.body: Two moves matter in French practice: faire opposition — calling your bank to block the card — and porter plainte, filing a complaint at the commissariat or online. If a purchase goes wrong rather than criminal, you invoke le droit de rétractation, the fourteen-day cooling-off period for distance selling, or la garantie.

examples.english: In case of a dispute, you can go to a mediator.

blocks.tip: Porter plainte contre X is the formal phrase when you don't know who the culprit is — X literally stands in for the unknown person.

blocks.heading: Il vaut mieux que + subjonctif
blocks.body: Il vaut mieux is the French way of saying "it's better" or "you'd better". With no change of subject, use il vaut mieux + infinitive. As soon as you name who should act, switch to il vaut mieux que + subjunctive. The same pattern works with il faut que, il est important que and il est préférable que — all expressions of necessity or advice.

blocks.tip: The four irregulars you need here: que je sois (être), que j'aie (avoir), que je fasse (faire), que j'aille (aller). Learn them as a block.

blocks.heading: Se faire + infinitif : when it happens to you
blocks.body: Se faire + infinitive expresses that something was done to you, whether you wanted it or not. Je me suis fait voler mon téléphone is far more natural than a passive. In the passé composé the auxiliary is être, but the participle fait never agrees. Se faire avoir is the frozen expression for being taken in.

passages.title: L'appel du faux conseiller
passages.french:
Un mardi soir, le téléphone de Sabine sonne : « Bonjour madame, service sécurité de votre banque. »
L'homme est calme, poli, et connaît son nom, son agence et les quatre derniers chiffres de sa carte.
« Nous avons détecté un paiement suspect de 890 euros à Marseille. Ce n'est pas vous ? »
Sabine, qui n'a jamais mis les pieds à Marseille, répond non, évidemment.
« Très bien. Pour bloquer l'opération, il faut simplement valider le refus dans votre application. »
Elle valide. En réalité, elle vient d'autoriser un virement de huit cent quatre-vingt-dix euros.
Ce n'est qu'une heure plus tard, devant son relevé, qu'elle comprend qu'elle s'est fait avoir.
Le lendemain, sa conseillère lui explique la règle : la banque n'appelle jamais pour faire valider quoi que ce soit.
Sabine a fait opposition, porté plainte au commissariat et envoyé toutes les captures d'écran comme preuves.
La banque l'a remboursée au bout de cinq semaines, après un long échange de courriers.
« Ce qui m'a piégée, ce n'est pas la naïveté », dit-elle. « C'est l'urgence : il ne m'a laissé aucune seconde pour réfléchir. »
Depuis, sa règle est simple : quand on la presse, elle raccroche et rappelle elle-même le numéro au dos de sa carte.
passages.english:
One Tuesday evening, Sabine's phone rings: "Good evening madam, your bank's security department."
The man is calm, polite, and knows her name, her branch and the last four digits of her card.
"We've detected a suspicious payment of 890 euros in Marseille. That isn't you?"
Sabine, who has never set foot in Marseille, says no, obviously.
"Very good. To block the transaction, you simply need to confirm the refusal in your app."
She confirms. In reality, she has just authorised a transfer of eight hundred and ninety euros.
Only an hour later, looking at her statement, does she realise she has been taken in.
The next day, her adviser explains the rule: the bank never calls to have you confirm anything.
Sabine blocked the card, filed a complaint at the police station and sent all the screenshots as evidence.
The bank refunded her after five weeks, following a long exchange of letters.
"What trapped me wasn't naivety," she says. "It was the urgency: he didn't leave me a single second to think."
Since then her rule is simple: when someone rushes her, she hangs up and calls back the number on the back of her card herself.
